entry.title: B300 vs B200: what does Blackwell Ultra add for training?
entry.summary: Blackwell Ultra adds memory, not BF16 or FP8 training speed. The NVIDIA B300 has 288 GB per GPU against the B200's 180 GB, with the same FP8 throughput and memory bandwidth. On Nodus the B300 is listed at $6.943/hr and the B200 at $5.50/hr, so a B300 must finish a job 1.26 times faster to cost less. Pick the B300 when its memory saves you a second node or CPU offloading, or when you train in NVFP4, and keep the B200 for everything else. The B300's other gains, faster FP4 and faster attention math, matter most for inference. They can help training, but only for jobs that use them. The rest of this post shows where the line falls, with a priced job and the memory math. Memory capacity, FP4 throughput, attention math and node networking went up. entry.title: How to compare AI image prices without fooling yourself
entry.summary: Answer: compare the same output specification, on the same date, and normalise three things first — the resolution behind the label, whether the price includes a quality axis, and whether references are charged per image. Skip any of the three and a cheaper model can cost more per delivered image. On Callirra image pricing looks like one number per image. It is usually three numbers wearing a coat: pixels, quality effort, and inputs. Here is the checklist I use before quoting anything. Pixels are the first place a comparison leaks. Two models can both advertise a tier and not return the same raster: One model's "1080P" may return 1920×1056 — a pixel-area cap, not a rounding error. entry.title: reset() Inside onSubmit Only Half-Resets a React Hook Form. Here's What Stays Behind
entry.summary: You save a form, call reset() in your submit handler, and the inputs go blank. Looks done. Then the user starts typing the next entry and a red "Title needs 3+ chars" shows up while they're still typing, on a form that's supposed to be fresh. The values were reset. The submission state wasn't. The React Hook Form reset docs spell this out in their rules: "Avoid calling reset inside onSubmit. handleSubmit updates isSubmitted, isSubmitSuccessful and submitCount after your handler finishes, so a reset there clears the values but not the submission state." So the order is: your handler runs, reset() clears everything, then handleSubmit finishes and writes "submitted, successful, count +1" back on top.
